Abstract
Humanoid robots possess exceptional potential due to their capacity to
perform versatile and human-like whole-body tasks. However, realizing
agile and coordinated motions remains challenging, primarily due to the
discrepancy in dynamics between simulations and real-world environments.
Current methodologies, including system identification (SysID) and do-
main randomization (DR), often demand extensive parameter tuning
efforts or yield overly cautious policies, thus compromising agility.
In this thesis, we introduce ASAP (Aligning Simulation and Real Physics),
a two-stage framework aimed at effectively addressing dynamics mis-
matches and enabling agile whole-body movements in humanoid robots.
During the first stage, motion-tracking policies are pre-trained in simula-
tion leveraging retargeted human motion data. In the second stage, policies
are deployed on a real-world humanoid robot to gather data for training a
delta (residual) action model, which compensates for simulation-to-reality
dynamics differences. Subsequently, ASAP fine-tunes the pre-trained
policies by incorporating the delta action model within the simulator,
resulting in improved alignment with real-world dynamics.
Our evaluation encompasses three distinct transfer scenarios: IsaacGym to
IsaacSim, IsaacGym to Genesis, and IsaacGym to the physical Unitree G1
humanoid robot. Results demonstrate that ASAP significantly enhances
agility and whole-body coordination compared to baseline approaches
such as SysID, DR, and traditional delta dynamics learning techniques.
By enabling highly agile and expressive motions previously challenging
to achieve, our approach underscores the effectiveness of delta action
learning in bridging the sim-to-real gap. This work highlights a promising
direction for advancing agile humanoid robotics.

Introduction
For decades, researchers have envisioned humanoid robots capable of achieving—or
even surpassing—human-level agility. Despite substantial progress, prior studies [19,
46, 47, 50, 73, 74, 95, 107] have primarily focused on locomotion tasks, viewing legs
predominantly as instruments for mobility. More recent efforts [10, 24, 25, 26, 32]
have expanded the focus towards whole-body expressiveness, particularly upper-body
movements, yet the agile and coordinated motions characteristic of human behavior
remain elusive. A significant hurdle in achieving agile whole-body humanoid skills
arises from inherent hardware limitations coupled with the persistent mismatch
between simulated dynamics and real-world physics.
Existing methodologies for addressing this simulation-to-reality gap broadly fall
into three categories: system identification (SysID), domain randomization (DR), and
learned dynamics approaches. SysID methods estimate essential physical parameters,
such as motor response characteristics, link masses, and terrain interactions [19, 102].
However, SysID methods typically depend on predefined parameter spaces [49],
making them prone to inaccuracies when encountering dynamics not captured within
the modeled distribution. Moreover, SysID often necessitates ground truth torque
measurements [29], which are typically unavailable on common hardware platforms,
thus restricting practical use. Alternatively, DR methods attempt to bridge the
dynamics mismatch by extensively randomizing simulation parameters during policy
training [59, 68, 79, 85, 87].
However, this randomization tends to yield overly

Motivated by these limitations, this thesis proposes ASAP, a two-stage rein-

1. We introduce ASAP, an effective RL-based sim-to-real alignment framework
that leverages a delta action model trained with real-world robot data.
2. We demonstrate successful real-world deployment of RL-based whole-body
control policies, achieving agile and dynamic humanoid movements previously
unattainable.
3. Extensive experimental evaluations across multiple scenarios confirm that ASAP
significantly reduces dynamics mismatch and tracking errors, facilitating highly
agile humanoid robot skills.
4. To support further research and seamless transfer between simulation platforms,

Background
2.1
Learning-based Humanoid Control
In recent years, learning-based methods have made significant progress in whole-
body control for humanoid robots.
Primarily leveraging reinforcement learning
algorithms [80] within physics simulators [58, 63, 88], humanoid robots have learned
a wide range of skills, including robust locomotion [19, 44, 45, 47, 48, 73, 74, 98, 106],
jumping [46], and parkour [50, 107]. More advanced capabilities, such as dancing [10,
32, 105], loco-manipulation [15, 24, 25, 53], and even backflipping [78], have also been
demonstrated. Meanwhile, the humanoid character animation community has achieved
highly expressive and agile whole-body motions in physics-based simulations [55, 71,
86], including cartwheels [67], backflips [69], sports movements [56, 90, 91, 92, 104],
and smooth object interactions [17, 22, 86].
However, transferring these highly
dynamic and agile skills to real-world humanoid robots remains challenging due to
the dynamics mismatch between simulation and real-world physics. To address this
challenge, our work focuses on learning and compensating for this dynamics mismatch,
enabling humanoid robots to perform expressive and agile whole-body skills in the
real world.

Abstract
Humanoid robots possess exceptional potential due to their capacity to
perform versatile and human-like whole-body tasks. However, realizing
agile and coordinated motions remains challenging, primarily due to the
discrepancy in dynamics between simulations and real-world environments.
Current methodologies, including system identification (SysID) and do-
main randomization (DR), often demand extensive parameter tuning
efforts or yield overly cautious policies, thus compromising agility.
In this thesis, we introduce ASAP (Aligning Simulation and Real Physics),
a two-stage framework aimed at effectively addressing dynamics mis-
matches and enabling agile whole-body movements in humanoid robots.
During the first stage, motion-tracking policies are pre-trained in simula-
tion leveraging retargeted human motion data. In the second stage, policies
are deployed on a real-world humanoid robot to gather data for training a
delta (residual) action model, which compensates for simulation-to-reality
dynamics differences. Subsequently, ASAP fine-tunes the pre-trained
policies by incorporating the delta action model within the simulator,
resulting in improved alignment with real-world dynamics.
Our evaluation encompasses three distinct transfer scenarios: IsaacGym to
IsaacSim, IsaacGym to Genesis, and IsaacGym to the physical Unitree G1
humanoid robot. Results demonstrate that ASAP significantly enhances
agility and whole-body coordination compared to baseline approaches
such as SysID, DR, and traditional delta dynamics learning techniques.
By enabling highly agile and expressive motions previously challenging
to achieve, our approach underscores the effectiveness of delta action
learning in bridging the sim-to-real gap. This work highlights a promising
direction for advancing agile humanoid robotics.

Introduction
For decades, researchers have envisioned humanoid robots capable of achieving—or
even surpassing—human-level agility. Despite substantial progress, prior studies [19,
46, 47, 50, 73, 74, 95, 107] have primarily focused on locomotion tasks, viewing legs
predominantly as instruments for mobility. More recent efforts [10, 24, 25, 26, 32]
have expanded the focus towards whole-body expressiveness, particularly upper-body
movements, yet the agile and coordinated motions characteristic of human behavior
remain elusive. A significant hurdle in achieving agile whole-body humanoid skills
arises from inherent hardware limitations coupled with the persistent mismatch
between simulated dynamics and real-world physics.
Existing methodologies for addressing this simulation-to-reality gap broadly fall
into three categories: system identification (SysID), domain randomization (DR), and
learned dynamics approaches. SysID methods estimate essential physical parameters,
such as motor response characteristics, link masses, and terrain interactions [19, 102].
However, SysID methods typically depend on predefined parameter spaces [49],
making them prone to inaccuracies when encountering dynamics not captured within
the modeled distribution. Moreover, SysID often necessitates ground truth torque
measurements [29], which are typically unavailable on common hardware platforms,
thus restricting practical use. Alternatively, DR methods attempt to bridge the
dynamics mismatch by extensively randomizing simulation parameters during policy
training [59, 68, 79, 85, 87].
However, this randomization tends to yield overly
conservative policies [25], hindering the attainment of high agility. Lastly, learned

low-dimensional robotic systems, such as drones [81] and ground vehicles [97], yet
their effectiveness for humanoid robots remains largely unexplored.
Motivated by these limitations, this thesis proposes ASAP, a two-stage rein-
forcement learning (RL) framework designed explicitly to align simulated dynamics
with real-world physics, thereby enabling agile whole-body humanoid behaviors. In
the pre-training stage, we train base policies in simulation by leveraging human
motion capture data. Specifically, human motions are retargeted onto humanoid robot
models [25], after which a phase-conditioned policy [67] is trained to closely track
these retargeted movements. Nonetheless, directly transferring this policy to physical
hardware results in notable performance degradation due to dynamics discrepancies.
To mitigate this challenge, the post-training stage employs real-world rollout
data collected from the humanoid robot, including proprioceptive states and positional
data captured via a motion capture system. This data is subsequently replayed in

simulation, exposing the dynamics mismatch through observed tracking errors. A
delta action model, trained via supervised learning on these discrepancies, is then
developed to predict residual actions required to compensate for real-world dynamics
variations. This learned residual effectively bridges the simulation-to-reality gap.
Finally, the pre-trained policy undergoes fine-tuning within the augmented simulation
environment, incorporating the delta action model to adapt robustly to real-world
physics.
We rigorously validate ASAP through extensive experiments, showcasing agile
whole-body skills on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot [77]. Experimental results
demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses baseline methods (SysID, DR,
and traditional learned dynamics) in terms of motion tracking accuracy, evaluated
across both sim-to-sim scenarios (IsaacGym to IsaacSim, IsaacGym to Genesis) and
sim-to-real transfers (IsaacGym to Real).
The primary contributions of this thesis are as follows:
1. We introduce ASAP, an effective RL-based sim-to-real alignment framework
that leverages a delta action model trained with real-world robot data.
2. We demonstrate successful real-world deployment of RL-based whole-body
control policies, achieving agile and dynamic humanoid movements previously

Background
2.1
Learning-based Humanoid Control
In recent years, learning-based methods have made significant progress in whole-
body control for humanoid robots.
Primarily leveraging reinforcement learning
algorithms [80] within physics simulators [58, 63, 88], humanoid robots have learned
a wide range of skills, including robust locomotion [19, 44, 45, 47, 48, 73, 74, 98, 106],
jumping [46], and parkour [50, 107]. More advanced capabilities, such as dancing [10,
32, 105], loco-manipulation [15, 24, 25, 53], and even backflipping [78], have also been
demonstrated. Meanwhile, the humanoid character animation community has achieved
highly expressive and agile whole-body motions in physics-based simulations [55, 71,
86], including cartwheels [67], backflips [69], sports movements [56, 90, 91, 92, 104],
and smooth object interactions [17, 22, 86].
However, transferring these highly
dynamic and agile skills to real-world humanoid robots remains challenging due to
the dynamics mismatch between simulation and real-world physics. To address this
challenge, our work focuses on learning and compensating for this dynamics mismatch,
enabling humanoid robots to perform expressive and agile whole-body skills in the
real world.

2.2
Offline and Online System Identification
The dynamics mismatch between simulators and real-world physics can be attributed
to two primary factors: inaccuracies in the robot model descriptions and the presence
of complex real-world dynamics that are difficult for physics-based simulators to
capture. Traditional approaches address these issues using system identification
(SysID) methods [5, 39], which calibrate the robot model or simulator based on
real-world performance.
These methods can be broadly categorized into offline
SysID and online SysID, depending on whether system identification occurs at test
time. Offline SysID methods typically collect real-world data and adjust simulation
parameters to train policies in more accurate dynamics. The calibration process may
focus on modeling actuator dynamics [29, 85, 99], refining robot dynamics models [2,
18, 21, 30, 36], explicitly identifying critical simulation parameters [9, 13, 96, 102],
learning a distribution over simulation parameters [4, 27, 75], or optimizing system
parameters to maximize policy performance [64, 76]. Online SysID methods, in
contrast, aim to learn a representation of the robot’s state or environment properties,
enabling real-time adaptation to different conditions. These representations can
be learned using optimization-based approaches [43, 70, 101, 103], regression-based
methods [14, 19, 31, 40, 41, 42, 60, 61, 62, 72, 89, 100], next-state reconstruction
techniques [51, 54, 65, 83, 94], direct reward maximization [47], or by leveraging
tracking and prediction errors for online adaptation [16, 28, 57, 66]. Our framework
takes a different approach from traditional SysID methods by learning a residual
action model that directly compensates for dynamics mismatch through corrective
actions, rather than explicitly estimating system parameters.
2.3
Residual Learning for Robotics
Learning a residual component alongside learned or pre-defined base models has been
widely used in robotics. Prior work has explored residual policy models that refine the
actions of an initial controller [1, 3, 8, 12, 20, 33, 34, 42, 84]. Other approaches leverage
residual components to correct inaccuracies in dynamics models [23, 35, 38, 66, 82]
or to model residual trajectories resulting from residual actions [11] for achieving
precise and agile motions. RGAT [35] uses a residual action model with a learned

RL-based residual actions to align the dynamics mismatch between simulation and

Asymmetric Actor-Critic Architecture
Given the inherent partial observability
of real-world humanoid tasks, we adopt an asymmetric actor-critic training paradigm.
The critic network is provided privileged information such as global reference positions
and root linear velocities, enhancing value estimation stability. In contrast, the
actor receives only realistic proprioceptive information and the phase variable. This
design ensures that the policy remains robust during real-world deployment, where
privileged observations (e.g., perfect odometry) are unavailable, thus overcoming
known deployment issues in previous work [24, 25].
Progressive Termination Curriculum
Tracking complex agile motions, such
as jumps and flips, is challenging due to high initial difficulty. We address this by
introducing a progressive termination curriculum that starts with a lenient tracking
error tolerance (1.5 meters) and gradually tightens to a stricter threshold (0.3 meters)
as training progresses. This strategy allows the policy to first master basic balance

Real-World Data. In the real-world experiments, we prioritize both motion

scenarios.

Conclusions
While ASAP demonstrates promising results in bridging the sim-to-real gap for agile
humanoid control, our framework has several real-world limitations that highlights
critical challenges in scaling agile humanoid control to real-world:
• Hardware Constraints: Agile whole-body motions exert significant stress on
robots, leading to motor overheating and hardware failure during data collection.
Two Unitree G1 robots were broken to some extent during our experiments.
This bottleneck limits the scale and diversity of real-world motion sequences
that can be safely collected.
• Dependence on Motion Capture Systems: Our pipeline requires MoCap
setup to record real-world trajectories. This introduces practical deployment
barriers in unstructured environments where MoCap setups are unavailable.
• Data-Hungry Delta Action Training: While reducing the delta action
model to 4 DoF ankle joints improved sample efficiency, training the full 23 DoF
model remains impractical for real-world deployment due to the large demand
of required motion clips (e.g., > 400 episodes in simulation for the 23 DoF delta
action training).
Future directions could focus on developing damage-aware policy to mitigate hardware
risks, leveraging MoCap-free alignment to eliminate the reliance on MoCap, and
exploring adaptation techniques for delta action models to achieve sample-efficient
few-shot alignment.
